title: Competitive notes (rough): marketplace alternatives + positioning for latency/cost controls + Private deployments
content:
Context / why this doc exists
- Pulling together rough competitive notes specifically for AWS + GCP marketplace buyers.
- Goal is NOT a full battlecard. This is focused on: (1) what buyers compare us against when procurement wants marketplace, and (2) how we position Redwood’s latency/cost controls + Dedicated/Private deployments without making risky claims.
- Audience: PMM/Marketing drafting listing copy + FAQ, Sales/SEs handling procurement-led evals.

Quick framing for marketplace buyers
- Typical buyer intent:
  - “I want to buy the LLM part the same way I buy everything else: via AWS/GCP marketplace. Make it easy to subscribe + get invoiced + satisfy security review.”
  - Often already running some workloads on Bedrock/Vertex endpoints or doing DIY on EKS/GKE.
  - They are sensitive to: predictable spend, predictable performance, security posture, and operational overhead.
- Redwood’s main wedge in marketplace:
  - Unified inference platform with production controls (latency/cost/reliability) across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
  - “You can start fast (Hosted), lock in predictable throughput (Dedicated), and move into your environment when needed (Private) without re-architecting.”

Competitive set (marketplace-adjacent) and what they usually pitch

1) Cloud-native managed model endpoints (AWS Bedrock / SageMaker / GCP Vertex AI)
- Why buyers choose them:
  - Native procurement and billing (already in their cloud bill).
  - Easy identity/network controls (IAM, VPC, org policies), familiar security model.
  - “Single throat to choke” perception.
- Typical weaknesses we can (carefully) highlight:
  - Less portability / more lock-in to that cloud’s serving layer.
  - Limited transparency and knobs for unit economics (depends on product; often hard to reason about cost per token by workload shape).
  - Dedicated capacity options exist, but often feel like separate products/flows; rollout + eval tooling not always first-class.
- Redwood positioning vs cloud-native endpoints:
  - “Cloud billing convenience + dedicated focus on inference economics.”
  - Emphasize operational tooling: token-level breakdowns, request routing policies, rollouts (canary/A-B), fallback policies.
  - Private deployments: “Run the same API/runtime in your VPC/on-prem when compliance requires, rather than rewriting around a different endpoint model.”
- Landmines:
  - Avoid claiming “faster than Bedrock/Vertex” broadly. Keep to “optimized runtime + workload-aware batching/caching/quantization recommendations” and “predictable performance profiles.”

2) LLM API providers (general hosted APIs)
- Why buyers choose them:
  - Fast start, great docs, minimal infra.
  - Model access breadth.
- Typical buyer objections we hear in procurement-led flows:
  - Data handling concerns, residency, retention defaults.
  - Need dedicated capacity / SLAs.
  - Want VPC/on-prem option; or at least strong shared responsibility clarity.
- Redwood positioning:
  - “API-first experience, but with enterprise deployment modes and cost controls.”
  - Marketplace angle: “procurement-friendly path + clear entitlements + metering.”
  - Strongly highlight Dedicated + Private as progression paths.
- Landmines:
  - Don’t name competitor pricing or imply we are always cheaper; speak in terms of controls that reduce unit cost.

3) ‘Inference platforms’ and model hosting vendors (often show up in enterprise bake-offs)
- Why buyers consider them:
  - They want an abstraction layer over different open models.
  - Some offer fine-tuning + deployment bundles.
- Where Redwood should differentiate (specific to marketplace):
  - “Production runtime + ops layer” not just model access.
  - Clear separation of modes: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with consistent API.
  - Better story for graceful degradation: routing + fallback when capacity constrained.
- Notes:
  - Many of these vendors have marketplace listings but their SKUs can be confusing (tokens vs seats vs ‘credits’). We should emphasize SKU clarity tied to usage and/or capacity.

4) DIY self-hosting on EKS/GKE (vLLM/TGI + custom glue)
- Why buyers go DIY:
  - Cost control at scale.
  - Data control / compliance.
  - Skepticism of vendor lock-in.
- Real enterprise pain points DIY teams run into:
  - SRE burden: capacity planning, autoscaling, GPU fragmentation, on-call.
  - Release/rollout safety (model versioning, canaries) becomes bespoke.
  - Hard to measure token-level economics and regressions; “we built dashboards” but inconsistent.
  - Multi-region / failover complexity.
- Redwood positioning:
  - Private deployment as “bring-your-own-environment without bringing-your-own-inference-platform.”
  - Emphasize shared responsibility + audit logs + KMS integrations + configurable retention.
  - “We provide the runtime + control plane + observability; you keep the environment boundaries.”
- Landmines:
  - Avoid “replace your platform team.” Better: “reduce undifferentiated ops work; keep control where it matters.”

Marketplace-specific competitive dynamics
- Marketplace competitor is often not a single vendor; it’s the path of least resistance:
  - If we make subscription → entitlement → org provisioning slow/confusing, buyers fall back to whatever’s already in their cloud account.
- Therefore, our listing must do two jobs:
  1) Prove we can satisfy security + procurement quickly.
  2) Make the product differentiation obvious in <2 minutes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private).

How we should position: the 3 pillars (suggested copy scaffolding)

Pillar A: Predictable performance (latency + throughput) with explicit controls
- Talk tracks:
  - “Workload-aware batching/caching and optimized runtime paths to meet latency SLOs while improving throughput.”
  - “Dedicated capacity available when you need predictable throughput and isolation.”
  - “Smart routing + fallback policies help keep apps online.”
- Proof points to reference (without over-claiming):
  - Token-level cost + latency breakdowns in Console.
  - Per-model performance profiles (Redwood-verified) and version pinning.

Pillar B: Unit economics you can actually manage (cost controls, not just pricing)
- Talk tracks:
  - “Reduce per-token cost via batching, caching, and quantization guidance; make tradeoffs visible.”
  - “Observability that ties latency/cost back to routes, models, and prompt shapes.”
  - “Optimize toolkit provides recommendations and regression alerts tied to eval sets.”
- Common marketplace buyer hook:
  - “Your procurement team cares about invoice consolidation; your engineers care about cost per successful outcome. We address both.”

Pillar C: Deployment flexibility (Hosted → Dedicated → Private) without re-platforming
- Talk tracks:
  - “Start with Hosted for fastest onboarding; move to Dedicated for predictable throughput/data isolation; deploy Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated workloads.”
  - “Same API + consistent operational tooling across environments.”
- Enterprise security hooks:
  - “KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, retention controls, shared responsibility clarity.”
  - “Private control plane option + customer-managed networking.”

Competitive comparisons (practical)

When buyer says: “We can just use Bedrock / Vertex since it’s already approved.”
- Response framing:
  - Agree: “If the primary requirement is ‘native cloud service already approved,’ those can be great.”
  - Pivot: “Where teams get stuck is meeting strict latency SLOs while controlling unit cost and managing model rollouts safely.”
  - Offer: “We can integrate into your procurement path via marketplace and still give you dedicated inference-focused controls + Private option.”
- Ask questions:
  - “Do you have a latency SLO per route? Are you tracking cost per route/model?”
  - “Do you need dedicated throughput?”
  - “Any future requirement for VPC/on-prem?”

When buyer says: “We already self-host open models on EKS/GKE.”
- Response framing:
  - “Great — you’ve already proven the workload.”
  - “Private is designed for teams exactly at that stage: keep your environment boundary, reduce the ops and rollout risk.”
- Ask questions:
  - “How do you do canaries and rollbacks today?”
  - “How often do you have capacity incidents or latency spikes due to batching/queueing?”
  - “How do you audit access and retain logs for compliance?”

When buyer says: “We just need an API like Provider X; why add another platform?”
- Response framing:
  - “If you only need a quick prototype, any hosted API works.”
  - “In production, the hard parts are cost predictability, performance under load, enterprise controls, and deployment flexibility.”
  - “Marketplace SKUs + entitlements give you procurement compliance; Dedicated/Private give you options when requirements change.”

Do / Don’t language (listing-safe)
- Do:
  - “Optimize latency and cost with batching/caching guidance and observability.”
  - “Support Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with a consistent API.”
  - “Provide audit logs, encryption, and configurable retention controls (see security documentation).”
  - “SLA-backed options available (Dedicated/enterprise support tiers).”
- Don’t:
  - “Guaranteed fastest/cheapest vs {cloud vendor}.”
  - “We are SOC 2 certified” unless the exact wording is approved by Security/GRC (use approved phrasing from the security packet and link).
  - “No data is ever stored” (too absolute; defer to retention policy defaults + configurability).

Notes on screenshots/diagrams that help win competitive comparisons
- A single diagram showing 3 boxes: Hosted / Dedicated / Private, all behind one API + Console.
- Console screenshot showing:
  - Token-level cost & latency breakdown by route/model.
  - Rollout controls (canary/A-B) + fallback policy.
  - Audit log export / security settings (if approved for public listing).

Open questions / to validate (before we freeze copy)
- Which competitor names are allowed in internal-only enablement vs marketplace copy? (assume: marketplace listing should stay category-based; enablement can be more explicit.)
- What performance “proof” can we safely cite in public materials (benchmarks, kernel optimizations, etc.) without triggering partner review issues?
- Confirm exact approved security phrasing: SOC2/ISO posture wording, encryption at rest/in transit, KMS integrations, retention defaults.

Action items (PMM/GTM)
- Soojin: translate Pillar A/B/C into 3 short blocks for listing + 6 FAQ answers.
- Markus (SE): provide 3 real customer anecdotes (anonymized) illustrating (1) Dedicated for predictable throughput, (2) Private for compliance, (3) cost controls prevented a runaway bill.
- Naomi (Security): review Don’t statements + provide approved security language snippets for listing/FAQ.
- Camila/Alex: ensure diagrams and screenshots align with what’s publishable (no internal-only metrics, no customer names).

Personal note (drafting guidance)
- Marketplace buyers are skimmers. If we don’t clearly answer “What is it?” and “How is it different from cloud endpoints?” in the first screen, we lose. Lead with deployment modes + economics controls, then let security docs do the rest.
